extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys and agents) preparing or litigating ex parte appeals before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and presenting ex parte appeals to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, including procedural prerequisites, briefing and oral advocacy strategy, timing, costs, and post-decision options. Designed to help practitioners decide between RCE and appeal and to improve written and oral advocacy at the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the appeals process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to the Board; Argue to the Board (briefs and optional oral hearing); Board consideration; Board decision; Optional post-decision action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the multi-step process: file notice of appeal and briefs, optionally request oral hearing, rely on Board consideration and decision, then pursue post-decision options (RCE, rehearing, Federal Circuit, Supreme Court, or civil action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-member panel requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 6(c) requires a final decision by a minimum of a three-member panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to appeals, derivation, post-grant review, and inter partes review proceedings. Members are designated by the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may appeal to the Board (jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 134 defines who may appeal to the Board: patent applicants with claims 'twice rejected' may appeal from the primary examiner's decision; in ex-parte reexamination the patent owner may appeal unfavorable final decisions; in inter partes reexamination patent owner and third-party requester may appeal adverse rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your party and situation fall within §134 before filing; identify whether rejection is 'twice' or 'final' as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites to file an appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be twice or finally rejected and a Notice of Appeal must be filed. Pre-appeal review is available (implemented July 12, 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the rejection status, timely file the Notice of Appeal, and consider pre-appeal review options to potentially avoid full briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing sequence and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant files an appeal brief; examiner files an Examiner's answer; appellant files a reply brief; appellant may (optionally) request an oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the required sequence and observe page/time constraints; a reply brief is typically limited in scope (new arguments often not permitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of Board review
rubrics_metrics.description: Board reviews arguments and evidence for an error identified by the appellant to determine if the examiner’s findings and conclusions are supported by a preponderance of the evidence (Ex Parte Frye).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments to show examiner error and point to the preponderance of record evidence supporting your position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible Board dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may Affirm, Affirm-in-part, Reverse, Vacate (rare), Remand (rare), Dismiss (rare), or issue a New ground of rejection (37 C.F.R. § 41.50(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for any outcome and understand the implications of each (e.g., remand returns to examination corps; new grounds may require opportunity to respond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision options
rubrics_metrics.description: After Board decision: file an RCE to return to Examining Corps; request rehearing from same panel; appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (35 U.S.C. §141) and then potentially the U.S. Supreme Court; or bring a civil action in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia (35 U.S.C. §145).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose post-decision route based on objectives (e.g., seeking further prosecution, judicial review, or damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare RCE vs Appeal across key dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding between RCE and PTAB appeal, compare (a) decision makers, (b) scope of evidence and arguments, (c) timing, and (d) costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to choose the path most suitable for case facts: examiner continuity and potential for new evidence favor RCE; neutral judicial review and appellate record may favor appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision maker differences between RCE and PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: RCEs typically continue before the examiner of record; appeals to PTAB involve Pre-Appeal Brief Conferences and Appeal Conferences (three-examiner reviews) and ultimately are decided by three APJs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the advantage of a neutral panel vs. continued examination by the same examiner when selecting path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of evidence and argument limitations on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: On RCE, new evidence, new arguments, and certain new claim amendments can be presented. On appeal, new evidence and claim amendments are limited after filing; new arguments generally allowed only in the appeal brief (not in reply brief), unless Examiner's answer introduces a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to introduce new evidence or amendments, an RCE may be appropriate; preserve and present all arguments you want considered before appealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing expectations and the fast-track option
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical PTAB decision on appeal is about 12–13 months after appeal forwarding fee; RCE responses are about 2.5 months. Fast-Track appeals can reduce appeal decision to under 6 months in some cases; one-year fast-track briefing timelines are available for expedited handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quick resolution is desired, consider Fast-Track or streamlined briefing schedules; note that fast-track is not suitable for all appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and fees for RCE vs appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: RCE fees: 1st request and subsequent pricing shown; Appeals: Notice of appeal fee ($840/$420/$210), Appeal forwarding fee ($2,360/$1,180/$590), Fast-Track petition fee ($420 or $0 if COVID-related), request for oral hearing fee ($1,360/$680/$340); plus costs to prepare briefs and replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider filing and preparation costs along with expected time and outcome when choosing between RCE and appeal. Fees vary with entity status (undiscounted/small/micro).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-appeal brief conference and appeal conference usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-Appeal Brief Conference pilot and Appeal Conference are optional examiner conferences that may result in allowance or reopening without need for a full Examiner's answer; only 43% of appeals resulted in an Examiner’s Answer (FY2010–2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider requesting pre-appeal review and using appeal conferences as they frequently lead to allow/reopen outcomes and can avoid full briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of appeal beyond reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reversal, appellant receives patent term adjustment for entire appeal period (unlike RCE); appeals may also remove issues from the table in a post-grant challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh patent term adjustment and strategic benefits when deciding to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review prosecution history and pick issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary steps: review the prosecution history, decide which rejections and which claims to address, and identify your strongest arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target and prioritize issues; do not waste brief space on weak or irrelevant issues; focus on points most likely to show examiner error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and concision in briefs (no page limit but quality matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no limit on number of pages, BUT the clearer and more concise your arguments, the better your chances of prevailing. Present strongest arguments first and avoid diluting them with weaker ones. Any rejection you do not address cannot be argued later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize brief to be concise and impactful; prioritize strongest arguments early; ensure all rejections you wish to preserve are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested argument format
rubrics_metrics.description: Address each ground of rejection under a separate heading and identify the ground by claim number, statutory basis, and references. Example headings: 'Whether claims 1-3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. §103 over Reference A in view of Reference B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear headings that map to issues; include precise claim numbers, statutory provisions, and references to aid reviewer navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim grouping strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same argument applies to two or more claims, consider arguing the claims as a group under a single heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group claims when identical reasoning applies to avoid repetition; explicitly state when claims are argued together and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguing claims separately when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a separate heading or subheading for any claim you want the PTAB to consider separately (example shows separate subheadings A/B for different claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim has distinct issues or you want discrete treatment, make separate headings and explain differences clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and argumentative sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial burden rests with the examiner to clearly state reasons for the rejection; after the examiner satisfies that burden, the burden shifts to appellant to explain why the examiner erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure arguments to first show insufficiency or error in examiner reasoning, then explain why the examiner’s position is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always explain why — avoid unsubstantiated assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: For any argument of examiner error, ALWAYS give reasons to support your position; it is not persuasive to simply state that the examiner erred without explaining why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 'because, because, because' — substantive explanation and record citations for each assertion of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common successful arguments to show examiner error
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the examiner: misunderstood/mischaracterized the claimed invention or pending claims; misunderstood the cited prior art; or misunderstood or misapplied the law or legal basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments to fit one or more of these categories and support them with record evidence, specification citations, or legal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate examiner misinterpretation of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the examiner’s characterization of the claimed invention or interpretation of claim language is inconsistent with the specification (identify specific portions of the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific specification paragraphs and explain why the examiner’s interpretation of a claim limitation is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show prior art was misunderstood or does not disclose elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the examiner’s understanding of a prior art reference is incorrect — e.g., why the reference does not disclose or suggest a particular claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific comparisons between the claim limitation and the reference, showing gaps or differences in disclosure or motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show legal errors in examiner reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that the examiner failed to apply law correctly (examples: insufficient reasoning to combine references; improper hindsight/knowledge of the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statutory and case law principles to show where the examiner’s legal analysis is deficient; explain why a person of ordinary skill would not have combined references absent knowledge of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct the Board's attention to evidence in the record (prior art of record, affidavits/declarations from experts) that supports your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite declarations and explain how they support your position (e.g., expert explains why a person of ordinary skill would or would not do X). Reference record page numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case law and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: If aware of PTAB or federal court decisions that support your position, explain how the case applies to the facts and shows the examiner erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific precedents and apply them to the factual record; explain the legal connection to your arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing purpose and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: For PTAB hearings, all evidence and argument must already be in the record; new evidence and new arguments are not permitted. Hearings are usually like a Q&A focused on issues critical to the panel's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to persuade present record positions; don't attempt to introduce new matters at hearing; anticipate judge questions about dispositive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the PTAB judges' expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB judges sit in 3-judge panels, have legal and scientific training, come into hearings with knowledge of the technology, background, prior art, evidence and arguments of record, unresolved dispositive questions, and some preliminary conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the record directly, focus on issues important to the panel, and avoid theatrical courtroom performance — judges are concerned with the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote hearing logistics and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings are conducted remotely by video (during COVID-19); public may request live video access; judges have the record and counsel should refer to specific page numbers in briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare exhibits and references with page numbers in mind; ensure technology is ready; instruct presenters to reference record locations clearly for remote panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-person hearing logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings are generally public; at least one judge may appear live, others often appear remotely; there may be remote observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for mixed in-person/remote environments and potential public observation; coordinate appearances and participation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB hearing flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical flow: introductory remarks by presiding judge; counsel appearances; argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan opening remarks briefly and then focus on substantive argument and anticipated Q&A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your time effectively in oral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals arguments are typically 20 minutes; you may not exceed time unless authorized. Be organized and concise: background is typically unnecessary; think modular; roadmap critical issues and dive in; address weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a time-budgeted modular roadmap; prioritize key issues and be concise; explicitly address weaknesses rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible when judges interrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may jump in and ask questions in a different order — follow that lead. Judges ask about areas critical to their decision, and oral argument is an opportunity to persuade the panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt to judge direction, answer directly, and welcome questions; being responsive is effective even if it derails your roadmap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured approach to answering PTAB questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three steps to answer: (1) be sure you understand the question, (2) consider its importance to your case, (3) answer and address the opposing view. Do not evade — answer, ask to return after consideration, or explain irrelevance if not relevant (but be prepared to answer anyway).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-step framework in preparation and live questioning; if necessary, request to return to a question after reflection rather than evading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling hard questions and concessions
rubrics_metrics.description: All cases have weaknesses. Prepare ahead, concede where appropriate (concessions enhance credibility and save time), and if the hard question is not dispositive, explain why you still prevail either way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan tactical concessions to maintain credibility and prioritize time on dispositive issues; explain alternative bases for decision if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to the record and specific page numbers during hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges have a copy of the record; counsel should refer to specific page numbers in briefs during oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite record locations precisely so judges can follow and verify assertions quickly, especially in remote hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: LEAP eligibility and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal Experience and Advancement Program (LEAP) targets patent agents and attorneys newer to PTAB practice. To qualify, a practitioner must have three or fewer substantive oral arguments in any federal tribunal (including PTAB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LEAP grants additional argument time (typically up to 15 minutes) to the party; the LEAP practitioner must have a substantive role and time may be allocated between counsel. Use LEAP to obtain additional hearing time if eligible.
